topic_title: Environmental Ecology, Climate Change Conventions, COP Summits, Environmental Statutes, Pollution Control & Disaster Management
syllabus_mapping: Environmental Ecology and Climate Change: Concepts of Ecology, Ecosystems, Biodiversity conservation (In-situ: National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Biosphere Reserves; Ex-situ: Gene banks, Seed banks, Botanical gardens) - Climate Change: Greenhouse effect, Global warming, Ocean acidification, Ozone depletion (Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment) - International Environmental Treaties: UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement (COP21), Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), Panchamrit commitments (COP26), COP28 UAE Consensus, Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (30x30 target), Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, CITES, Bonn Convention on Migratory Species - Indian Environmental Legislation: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (2022 Amendment), Water Act, 1974, Air Act, 1981, Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023, National Green Tribunal (NGT) Act, 2010 - Pollution Control & Waste Management: Air Quality Index (AQI), National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), Plastic Waste Management Rules, Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), E-waste and Hazardous waste management - Disaster Management: Disaster Management Act, 2005, NDMA, NDRF, SDMA, Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030), Coastal hazards, cyclones, and flood disaster resilience in Andhra Pradesh.

content.text: Ecology, Climate Governance, Global Environmental Treaties, Indian Statutory Architecture, and Disaster Risk Reduction

Environmental conservation and climate change adaptation represent the foremost existential challenges of the Anthropocene. India balances urgent developmental imperatives with global climate commitments, maintaining a comprehensive statutory apparatus under the Environment (Protection) Act and pioneering global climate diplomacy from the Paris Agreement to the COP26 Panchamrit pledges.

content.text: 1. International Climate Conventions: From Rio to COP28

content.caption: Milestones in Global Climate Change Governance
rows: UNFCCC (Rio Earth Summit, 1992)
Framework convention; established principle of 'Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities' (CBDR-RC).
Differentiated obligations between Annex I (developed historical emitters) and non-Annex I (developing countries like India).
Kyoto Protocol (COP3, 1997)
Legally binding emission cuts for developed nations; Clean Development Mechanism (CDM).
India participated actively in CDM carbon credit generation projects without mandatory domestic reduction caps.
Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015)
Limit global temperature rise well below 2.0°C and pursue 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels; nationally determined contributions (NDCs).

India submitted updated NDCs: reduce GDP emissions intensity by 45% by 2030 (from 2005 levels), achieve 50% non-fossil electric capacity by 2030, and create 2.5–3 billion tonnes CO2 equivalent carbon sink.
Glasgow COP26 (2021) & Panchamrit
Five-point climate pledge announced by India; Net Zero by 2070; phasedown of unabated coal power.
Formalized Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) promoting circular consumption patterns.
COP28 UAE Consensus (2023)
Operationalization of the Loss and Damage Fund; first Global Stocktake; agreed to 'transition away from fossil fuels' in energy systems.
India championed renewable tripling while safeguarding coal-based base-load power for national energy poverty alleviation.

content.caption: Key Environmental Statutes and Regulatory Authorities in India
rows: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (Amended 2022)
National Board for Wildlife (NBWL), Central Zoo Authority, NTCA (Project Tiger).
Rationalized schedules from 6 to 4; incorporated CITES provisions for endangered species trade regulation; established penal protections for protected areas.
Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 & Air Act, 1981
Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State Pollution Control Boards (APPCB).
Empowered to set effluent and emission standards, inspect industrial units, issue consent to establish (CTE) and operate (CTO), and shut down polluting units.
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
Enacted under Article 253 post-Bhopal Gas Tragedy as an umbrella environmental statute.
Powers to declare Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZs), formulate Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) notifications, and mandate Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA).
National Green Tribunal (NGT) Act, 2010
National Green Tribunal (NGT) with Principal Bench at New Delhi and Southern Bench at Chennai.

Specialized judicial forum established under Article 21 (Right to healthy environment); mandates time-bound disposal of environmental disputes within 6 months; applies Polluter Pays and Precautionary Principles.
Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC).
Exempts strategic defense infrastructure within 100 km of international borders from prior forest clearances; renamed 'Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam'.

content.text: 3. Disaster Risk Reduction & Coastal Vulnerability in Andhra Pradesh

items: Disaster Management Act, 2005: 3-tier disaster framework comprising NDMA (headed by Prime Minister), SDMA (headed by Chief Minister), and DDMA (headed by District Collector); established National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and dedicated mitigation funds (NDMF/SDMF).

Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030): Global non-binding framework outlining 4 priorities for action: understanding disaster risk, strengthening disaster risk governance, investing in resilience, and enhancing disaster preparedness for effective response and 'Build Back Better'.
Coastal Vulnerability in Andhra Pradesh: AP possesses a 974 km coastline highly vulnerable to Bay of Bengal tropical cyclones (e.g., Hudhud 2014, Titli 2018, Michaung 2023) and storm surges.

Disaster Mitigation Infrastructure: AP Disaster Recovery Project (APDRP), underground electrical cabling in Visakhapatnam, automated weather stations across mandals, Multi-Purpose Cyclone Shelters (MPCS), and real-time Early Warning Dissemination System (EWDS) sirens along coastal villages.

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Explain India's 'Panchamrit' climate pledges announced at COP26 Glasgow and its Updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement. How does India balance climate action with energy poverty? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Detail the five Panchamrit commitments: 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, meeting 50% energy requirement from renewables, reducing carbon emissions by 1 billion tonnes by 2030, cutting GDP carbon intensity by 45%, and achieving Net Zero by 2070; explain updated NDCs submitted to UNFCCC; analyze the ethical principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR); discuss the economic necessity of preserving base-load coal power while simultaneously scaling solar/green hydrogen to lift millions out of multidimensional energy poverty.

Critically evaluate the statutory role of the National Green Tribunal (NGT) in enforcing environmental jurisprudence in India. What are the key limitations in its functioning? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Outline NGT's establishment under the NGT Act 2010 pursuant to Article 21; discuss its specialized composition (judicial and expert scientific members); examine key environmental legal doctrines applied: Precautionary Principle, Polluter Pays Principle, and Sustainable Development; evaluate accomplishments: penalties on polluting municipalities, banning unscientific sand mining in rivers, enforcing solid waste management rules; analyze operational constraints: vacant judicial/expert posts, lack of independent institutional machinery to enforce contempt orders, and conflicts with High Courts under writ jurisdiction.

Analyze the cyclone vulnerability of coastal Andhra Pradesh. Discuss the structural and non-structural disaster risk mitigation measures required to build climate-resilient coastal communities. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Explain geographic vulnerabilities: funnel-shaped Bay of Bengal, shallow bathymetry causing catastrophic storm surges, deltaic low-lying terrain; examine non-structural measures: Doppler Weather Radars (Visakhapatnam, Machilipatnam), IMD color-coded cyclone alerts, Early Warning Dissemination System (EWDS), community-based disaster management teams; examine structural measures: Multi-Purpose Cyclone Shelters (MPCS), bio-shields (mangrove restoration in Coringa and Krishna delta, casuarina plantations), saline embankments, and underground electrical cable networks in coastal cities like Visakhapatnam.

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. At the COP26 Climate Summit in Glasgow (2021), Prime Minister Narendra Modi committed India to achieving Net-Zero greenhouse gas emissions by which target year?
(a) 2050
(b) 2060
(c) 2070
(d) 2080
Correct Answer: (c) 2070 [Explanation: India pledged at COP26 to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by the year 2070 as part of its Panchamrit commitments.]

Q2. The National Green Tribunal (NGT) was established in 2010 under which constitutional provision giving effect to the right to a healthy environment?
(a) Article 14
(b) Article 19(1)(a)
(c) Article 21
(d) Article 32
Correct Answer: (c) Article 21 [Explanation: The NGT was enacted to provide effective judicial relief in environmental matters, drawing constitutional legitimacy from Article 21 (Protection of life and personal liberty, interpreted to encompass a healthy environment).]

Q3. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework adopted at COP15 of the CBD set which flagship target to protect 30% of the world's land and oceans by 2030?
(a) 20x20 Target
(b) 30x30 Target
(c) 50x50 Target
(d) Zero Extinction Target
Correct Answer: (b) 30x30 Target [Explanation: Target 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) is known as the '30x30 target'—aiming to conserve at least 30% of terrestrial, inland water, and coastal/marine areas by 2030.]

Q4. Under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, who serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of the District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA)?
(a) Superintendent of Police
(b) District Collector / District Magistrate
(c) Mayor of the District Headquarters
(d) Zilla Parishad Chairperson
Correct Answer: (b) District Collector / District Magistrate [Explanation: Section 25 of the DM Act 2005 provides that the District Collector/District Magistrate/Deputy Commissioner shall be the Chairperson of the DDMA.]

Q5. Which mangrove sanctuary in Andhra Pradesh, located at the mouth of the Godavari River, constitutes the second-largest mangrove forest in India after the Sundarbans?
(a) Krishna Mangrove Sanctuary
(b) Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary
(c) Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary
(d) Nelapattu Bird Sanctuary
Correct Answer: (b) Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary [Explanation: Coringa Wildlife Sanctuary in Kakinada district encompasses the second-largest expanse of mangrove forests on the east coast of India.]
